kernels.l1: A complex number is two instructions: go across, then turn.
kernels.l2: A complex number is a pair of instructions — how far across, and how far up. Every ordinary number is one of these with no up at all.
kernels.l3: A complex number is written a + bi, where a and b are ordinary numbers and i is the new number with i × i = −1. Every ordinary number is a complex number with b = 0.
kernels.l4: A complex number is written a + bi: a real number, plus a real number times i, where i multiplied by itself gives −1. Those two reals are its real part and its imaginary part.
kernels.l5: A complex number is fixed by two ordinary reals — its real part and its imaginary part. The reals sit inside the complex numbers as the ones whose imaginary part is zero.
kernels.l6: A complex number is a pair of reals with a multiplication attached. The real part and the imaginary part are both ordinary real numbers, and the pair determines the number.
kernels.l7: A complex number is a real part plus i times an imaginary part, both real, with i squaring to −1. The reals sit inside as the numbers whose imaginary part is zero.
kernels.l8: A complex number is an across part and an up part, and two are equal exactly when both parts match. The system can be built honestly from ordered pairs, so i squaring to −1 is a calculation rather than a decree.
